questions.q: Acetaldehyde is warmed with diethyl malonate in the presence of piperidine. The product normally isolated is:
questions.explain: The Knoevenagel condensation includes the dehydration step, so the C=C product diethyl ethylidenemalonate is the answer. The β-hydroxy adduct is only an intermediate, which is the common trap.

questions.q: Arrange the active methylene compounds in order of decreasing acidity of the CH₂ group: (I) diethyl malonate, (II) ethyl acetoacetate, (III) acetylacetone.
questions.explain: The approximate pKa values are 9 for acetylacetone, 11 for ethyl acetoacetate and 13 for diethyl malonate. A lower pKa means a more acidic CH₂, so III > II > I.

questions.q: Crotonaldehyde is heated with malonic acid in pyridine (Doebner modification). The product is:
questions.explain: With malonic acid in pyridine the condensation is followed by loss of CO₂, leaving one COOH; crotonaldehyde gives sorbic acid. Penta-2,4-dienoic acid comes from acrolein and cinnamic acid from benzaldehyde.

questions.q: Why is a weak amine such as piperidine, rather than a strong base, used in the Knoevenagel condensation?
options: A strong base cannot deprotonate an active methylene compound
A strong base would also form the enolate of the aldehyde or ketone and cause its self-condensation
The amine is needed to hydrolyse the ester groups
A strong base would reduce the aldehyde to an alcohol
questions.explain: The active methylene CH₂ (pKa about 9–13) is acidic enough for an amine, while a simple ketone (pKa about 19) is barely touched. A strong base would deprotonate the carbonyl partner too and trigger self-condensation.
